rail_guard.text: Sligo, Sligeach, the shelly place. The railway came in 1862, three years before Yeats was born. As a boy he came here by train for the summers, and he wrote poems about the sea all his life.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited on this island. Where to?

then.text: I've finished it. 'Oh, Benbulben, you are large, and also you are stupendous.' It's a masterpiece. It has everything: mountain, adjective, hope.

else.text: I'm composing an ode to Benbulben. So far I have 'Oh, Benbulben, you are large.' It's rough, but the bones are strong.
Yeats said Sligo was 'the land of heart's desire'. I've yet to find the heart. I've found the desire. For tea.

options: 'You are large, and the rest is silence'

then.text: Hm. Fair enough. Poetry is slow. Come back when the muse has had her tea.
'Stupendous.' It scans. It's bold. I like a poem that doesn't apologise.

else.text: 'The rest is silence.' Ohh. That's Hamlet. That's a bit of a borrow. But I'll let it through. It suits a mountain.
Here. Take this. A hiker gave it to me for a haiku. It makes me rhyme. I'd rather you had it.

then.text: Benbulben's wearing a fog hat today. Very stylish. Very hard to climb.
Sun on Benbulben! Every ridge on the cliff stands out like corduroy.
No climbing in this wind, I'm afraid. The top's flat, and so would you be.

benbulben_guide.text: Benbulben's on top of an ancient seabed, with fossils all over. The flat top's about 526 metres, and the cliff face is a wall of limestone.
They say Diarmuid and Gráinne's story ended here: the wild boar and the hunter, and an old tale of love gone wrong. It's very Irish. Everything ends at a mountain.

then.text: Queen Maeve's cairn is in the clouds today. She likes her privacy.
Rain on Carrowmore. Five thousand years old, and still getting a wash.

knocknarea_fan.text: Over there, on Knocknarea, the huge cairn's said to be the grave of Queen Maeve. It's about 5,000 years old and hasn't been dug up. Nobody wants to disturb her.
Carrowmore's the megalithic cemetery. Some of it's older than Newgrange. I'm putting that in a postcard.

then.text: Doors open soon. Grab a seat, the play's short but the queue for ice cream isn't.

usher.text: The Hawk's Well Theatre is named for a Yeats play. He wrote it in 1916, inspired by Japanese Noh theatre. It's a play about a waiting man and a well with no water.
I wait all night. The play's quite short. I keep a flask.

then.text: Rain's grand for salmon. The river rises and they come up to see what's going on.
Dawn on the Garavogue. Best time for fishing. Worst time for talking, so whisper.

river_angler.text: The Garavogue runs through the middle of Sligo, only about four kilometres from Lough Gill to the sea. Salmon and sea trout come in all year.
Right in the middle of the town, and no one ever bothers me. They don't think I'm serious. I am.

then.text: Gale off the Atlantic! Massive waves at Strandhill. Mam says no. Mam's probably right.
Sun's out! The Atlantic's still freezing, but at least it's a pretty freezing.

surf_kid.text: {greeting} Strandhill's the surfing capital of Ireland, probably. Fifteen minutes up the road and the waves roll in forever.
You wear a thick wetsuit, because the Atlantic hasn't heard of summer. I've never been so cold and so happy.

then.text: Gallagher's eggs, a dozen a tray. He says there's a marten in somebody's Keeper team that used to be on his roof. He's very quiet about it.

else.text: Gallagher's eggs, a dozen a tray. Forty miles from here there's a hen keeper with a marten problem. I don't ask.

ct_marten_squirrel.text: A red squirrel on my bird table, first one in thirty years. They say it's the martens' doing. I'll take it, and I'll put wire on the henhouse.

ct_marten_wood.text: The Ghost goes by Gallagher's henhouse every dusk and tries the roof. He swears it sighs. I've heard it myself.
